title: The good of all
hook: the year ends where every Ardas ends, asking good for everyone

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking back at the depths: the Granth's themes, the Bhagats, history and grief, and your line, deep water, crossed. Today, the next to last day of the year, we end where every Ardas ends. Day three hundred thirty.

Amritsar, the 1700s, a spring morning at Vaisakhi. Riders come in from every direction: bands that spend the rest of the year scattered, sometimes quarreling, often hunted. For a few days they camp side by side, sit together before the Guru Granth Sahib, and decide things as one. That gathering had a name, which you met on day 289: the Sarbat Khalsa. Sarbat, everyone. Everyone who belonged. Every Ardas, to this day, ends with that same word. But in the prayer, it reaches a long way past the riders camped at Amritsar. Today: the good of all.
screen: `AMRITSAR, VAISAKHI, THE 1700S.` → `THE SARBAT KHALSA GATHERS.` → `THE SAME WORD, REACHING FURTHER.`

segments.voice: On day 251 we took the Ardas's last line apart: Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhane sarbat da bhala. Rising spirits through the Name, and, by your will, the good of all. Today, just one word from it, because you've now met that word twice. Sarbat. In the Sarbat Khalsa, it meant the whole Khalsa: every band, every leader, everyone who belonged, gathered before the Guru Granth Sahib. In the Ardas, the same word stretches past every border. Not the whole Khalsa. The whole of everything. Sarbat da bhala: the good of all, full stop. Now think about who says it. This year's path walked through a community hunted in the forests, massacred in 1746 and again in 1762, turned away from a harbor in 1914, attacked in its holiest place and in its own neighborhoods. The Ardas remembers much of that. And then it doesn't end with, protect our own, or, defeat our enemies. It ends by asking good for everyone, and Sikh teachers often say plainly that this includes the people who did the hurting. It grows out of what the Gurus taught: one light in every person; no enemy and no stranger, as Guru Arjan sings on Ang 1299. And notice tere bhane, by your will. The prayer doesn't tell God what everyone's good should look like. It asks, and leaves the shape of it to the Giver. That's a fitting place to stand at the end of a year: three hundred thirty days of stories, practices, the Japji and the depths, and a prayer whose last word reaches past the people saying it. For everyone, not just us.
screen: `SARBAT KHALSA: THE WHOLE KHALSA.` · `SARBAT DA BHALA: THE WHOLE OF EVERYTHING.` · `A HURT PEOPLE ASKS GOOD FOR ALL.` · `BY YOUR WILL, IN YOUR WAY.` · then, large: `FOR EVERYONE, NOT JUST US.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wish good for three people, chosen from this year. Settle, and breathe. First, someone who taught you something this year, in any way at all. Picture them, and wish them well, in your own words or none. Next, someone on the other side of a disagreement you're in, at home, at work, or in the news. Wish them well too, even a little. Last, someone far away whose story you heard on this path and will never meet. Wish them well. If you pray, you can hold all three in your prayer. If not, just hold them. The bell holds the time.
Sarbat. Everyone, the whole of everything — in sarbat da bhala, the last words of every Ardas, asking good for all.
Your line: for everyone, not just us. Today, do one small good thing for someone outside your circle, someone who can't pay you back. Day three hundred thirty.

howItsDone: Every Ardas, in every gurdwara and at home, ends with the line asking for chardi kala and sarbat da bhala, the good of all, before the congregation calls out the jaikara.

fork.setup: a community has been hurt again and again. its daily prayer is ending. what's the very last thing it asks for?
options: that it be kept safe from outsiders.
fork.reveal: every Ardas ends with sarbat da bhala: by your will, may all be well.

original.note: Gurmukhi: sarbat da bhala, the good of all; the last words of every Ardas.

trapdoor: what you thought: a community's prayer asks for its own people.
what it means: the Ardas ends, every time, by asking good for everyone, the people who hurt the community too.

what a scholar hears: the closing couplet belongs to the Ardas, not the Guru Granth Sahib; its wording was standardized in the Sikh Rehat Maryada, and it sums up the Gurus' teaching of the one light in all.

sources.quoted: Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhane sarbat da bhala

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1299 (no enemy, no stranger) and the teaching of the one light in all (paraphrased)
The Sarbat Khalsa gatherings at Amritsar at Vaisakhi and Diwali, 18th century

notes: The closing line of the Ardas is quoted in transliteration (traditional, public domain); the word-by-word gloss is a paraphrase. Confirm.

Removed the trapdoor claim that sarbat comes from Persian (its origin is debated; a Sanskrit link to sarvatra is also suggested). Trapdoor now notes the couplet is from the Ardas as standardized in the Sikh Rehat Maryada; confirm.
Teach changed 'the Gurus' last word' to 'the prayer's last word': the Ardas is a community prayer, not Gurbani, and its authorship is layered.
The practice invites wishing good for a difficult person; it is not a prayer text. Confirm tone.
Day 251 already taught sarbat da bhala; this day deliberately returns to it as the year's close.

Audit (second sample): the hook, teach and practice repeated day 251 almost point for point (the Ardas described, the line taken apart word by word, 'you'd expect anger', and the same loved one / stranger / difficult person practice), and the narrator spoke as a Sikh ('the people who hurt us', 'isn't about us'). Rewritten: the hook opens on the Sarbat Khalsa at Amritsar (day 289); the teach points back to day 251 for the gloss and takes one new angle, the word sarbat widening from the whole Khalsa to everyone; the practice keeps the outline's three people but chooses them from the year. Match, one myth and the trapdoor updated; first-person-plural narrator removed. Keeper: confirm 1746/1762, the 1914 harbor (Komagata Maru), Ang 1299 as Guru Arjan, and that Sikh teachers commonly say sarbat da bhala includes those who did harm.
